description: Independently authored cross-disciplinary gravitational-wave paleontology practice sets. Explanations and toy cases are educational, not new lab data or calibrated examinations.

sets.title: Binary orbits and binding energy
sets.summary: Relate orbital energy, angular momentum, period, eccentricity and survival without confusing one body's speed with relative motion.

objectives.title: Interpret energy and eccentricity
objectives.evidence: Separate bound Keplerian orbits, total orbital energy, and orbital shape.

questions.prompt: In the Newtonian point-mass two-body problem, a bound elliptical orbit has which relative mechanical energy?
choices: Positive
Negative
Exactly zero
questions.hint: Use the gravitational potential energy convention U(∞)=0.
questions.feedback: Relative orbital energy is negative for bound ellipses; zero is the parabolic threshold and positive corresponds to hyperbolic unbound motion.

questions.prompt: Two bound binaries have the same component masses and semi-major axis but different eccentricities. Their Keplerian orbital energies are:
choices: Different because an eccentric orbit always has more binding energy
Equal
Undetermined without the period
questions.hint: Recall E=−Gm₁m₂/(2a) for point masses.
questions.feedback: At fixed masses and semi-major axis, total Keplerian orbital energy is equal even though angular momentum and speed as a function of position differ.

questions.prompt: A test particle passes through pericentre on a bound eccentric Keplerian orbit. Which statement is supported?
choices: Its total orbital energy suddenly increases at pericentre.
Its orbital speed is greatest there, although its total orbital energy is constant.
Its radial velocity is largest at pericentre.
questions.hint: Use energy conservation and the fact that separation is smallest at pericentre.
questions.feedback: A smaller separation corresponds to a more negative potential energy and larger kinetic energy; the radial velocity vanishes at a turning point.

objectives.title: Calculate energies and speeds
objectives.evidence: Interpret E=−Gm₁m₂/(2a) and the vis-viva relation with correct held-fixed quantities.

questions.prompt: For the same component masses, a circular binary's semi-major axis halves. Its binding-energy magnitude changes by what factor?
choices: It halves.
It doubles.
It quadruples.
questions.hint: Binding-energy magnitude is proportional to 1/a.
questions.feedback: |E|=Gm₁m₂/(2a); halving a doubles |E| under the stated assumptions.

questions.prompt: A test body's circular orbital speed at radius r around a fixed central point mass M satisfies which relation?
choices: v²=GMr
v²=GM/r
v²=GM/r²
questions.hint: Balance GMm/r² with mv²/r.
questions.feedback: The centripetal acceleration is v²/r, giving v²=GM/r. G M/r² instead has acceleration units.

questions.prompt: Two point masses stay fixed while semi-major axis increases from a to 2a. E₂/E₁ equals:
questions.hint: Write both total orbital energies with their negative signs.
questions.feedback: E₂=−Gm₁m₂/(4a), E₁=−Gm₁m₂/(2a), hence E₂/E₁=1/2: the final orbit is less tightly bound.

objectives.title: Reason about sudden orbital changes
objectives.evidence: Use instantaneous separation, relative velocity and final masses to reason about a bound or unbound outcome.

questions.prompt: At an instantaneous symmetric mass-loss event, which quantities determine the immediately post-event point-mass relative orbital energy?
choices: The kick magnitude alone
Post-event total mass, separation and relative speed
Only the pre-event orbital period
questions.hint: Use ε=v_rel²/2−G M_after/r.
questions.feedback: The sign of ε depends jointly on post-event gravitational mass and the relative orbit at the event, not on one speed alone.

questions.prompt: Two identical pre-event binaries lose equal mass at different phases of their eccentric orbits. Why can outcomes differ?
choices: Eccentric orbits have no conserved energy.
Instantaneous separation and relative speed differ by orbital phase.
Mass loss always unbinds every eccentric binary.
questions.hint: Evaluate the energy immediately after the event using each event's r and v_rel.
questions.feedback: For equal mass changes, different event-phase values of r and relative velocity can change post-event energy and eccentricity.

questions.prompt: An initially bound binary receives a kick that reduces its relative speed, with masses and instantaneous separation fixed. Its immediate relative orbital energy:
choices: Must become positive.
Decreases (becomes more negative).
Is unchanged because the period has not updated.
questions.hint: Only the kinetic term changes at that instant.
questions.feedback: ε=v_rel²/2−GM/r: lowering speed lowers kinetic energy at fixed gravitational potential, while the new orbit can then be computed.

objectives.title: Check limits of the orbital model
objectives.evidence: Identify when simplified Keplerian formulae do not by themselves justify a physical conclusion.

questions.prompt: Can the circular-orbit relation v²=GM/r determine the speed at every point of an eccentric orbit?
choices: Yes; only r matters and energy is identical for every orbit.
No; use an eccentric-orbit relation such as vis-viva.
No; speed on an eccentric orbit is always constant.
questions.hint: Ask whether the trajectory is constrained to be circular.
questions.feedback: For an eccentric orbit, v²=GM(2/r−1/a) for relative motion; its semi-major axis also matters.

questions.prompt: Why is a remnant's velocity in the observer's frame insufficient to decide whether the binary survives?
choices: The observer's frame determines the gravitational constant.
Binding depends on the companion-relative velocity, masses and separation.
A positive absolute velocity makes every orbit unbound.
questions.hint: Switch to relative orbital coordinates.
questions.feedback: Bulk centre-of-mass motion can change individual frame velocities without changing the internal bound/unbound state.

questions.prompt: When using Keplerian orbital energy for a common-envelope interaction, what limitation should be stated?
choices: The point-mass formula exactly captures all envelope hydrodynamics.
Gas drag, mass exchange and energy transfer can invalidate isolated two-point-mass conservation during the interaction.
Conservation of energy never applies to gas.
questions.hint: Distinguish total energy conservation from constancy of the binary orbital energy alone.
questions.feedback: The orbital energy can transfer into gas and heat; isolated binary orbital energy need not remain constant during dissipative envelope evolution.

cases.title: Energy at a supernova
cases.scenario: A pre-event binary has r=1 (toy units), relative speed v=1, and post-event GM=0.6. Define ε=v²/2−GM/r.
cases.task: Compute ε and decide whether the post-event point-mass orbit is bound.
steps: Kinetic term is 1²/2=0.5.
Potential term is −0.6/1=−0.6.
ε=−0.1<0 in these units.
cases.solution: The two-body orbit is bound in this idealized instantaneous model; an actual binary also requires the correct post-event relative velocity and masses.

cases.title: Same energy, different shape
cases.scenario: Two point-mass binaries have identical m₁,m₂,a but eccentricities 0 and 0.7.
cases.task: Compare total energy, pericentre distance and angular momentum.
steps: Energy depends on a, not e: E=−Gm₁m₂/(2a) for both.
Pericentre is a(1−e): a versus 0.3a.
Angular momentum magnitude at fixed a is proportional to sqrt(1−e²).
cases.solution: Same orbital energy does not mean same closest approach or same angular momentum; eccentricity determines the latter two.

sources.title: The Evolution of Massive Binary Stars (review)

sets.title: Massive-star evolution and metallicity
sets.summary: Follow fuel burning, stellar winds, core collapse and metallicity-dependent pathways to remnants.

objectives.title: Build the stellar lifecycle
objectives.evidence: Differentiate main-sequence burning, post-main-sequence stages and compact-remnant formation.

questions.prompt: What powers a massive star throughout most of its main-sequence lifetime?
choices: A stable black-hole accretion disc.
Core hydrogen fusion.
Continuous helium fusion in the core from birth.
questions.hint: Name the defining nuclear-burning stage of the main sequence.
questions.feedback: Hydrogen fusion dominates the energy generation of main-sequence stars; later core burning stages follow after core hydrogen exhaustion.

questions.prompt: Why do more massive stars generally have shorter main-sequence lifetimes despite more fuel?
choices: Their initial hydrogen abundance is always zero.
Their luminosities and fuel-consumption rates increase strongly with mass.
They do not undergo hydrogen burning.
questions.hint: Compare available nuclear fuel with the rate of energy production.
questions.feedback: Main-sequence lifetime scales roughly as fuel divided by luminosity, and luminosity rises steeply with mass over much of the massive-star regime.

questions.prompt: A star's photospheric radius increases after it leaves the main sequence. Does that alone prove its helium core is already fusing?
choices: Yes; radius uniquely identifies the active core fuel.
No; shell burning and structural readjustment can expand the envelope before stable core helium ignition.
No; expansion always means no nuclear fusion anywhere.
questions.hint: Distinguish surface observables from the burning stage of the core.
questions.feedback: Post-main-sequence expansion can occur while hydrogen-shell burning supports luminosity; radius alone does not uniquely reveal central burning.

objectives.title: Compute timescale and mass budgets
objectives.evidence: Use mass-loss rates and dimensional reasoning without assuming a constant rate in a real star.

questions.prompt: A toy star loses 2 solar masses per million years for 3 million years at a constant rate. How much mass is lost?
choices: 2/3 solar mass.
6 solar masses.
1.5 solar masses.
questions.hint: Multiply rate by duration; this is a deliberately constant-rate toy model.
questions.feedback: ΔM=2 M☉/Myr ×3 Myr=6 M☉, assuming the rate is constant over the interval.

questions.prompt: If a star's luminosity is multiplied by 4 while its available nuclear fuel remains fixed, the fuel/L timescale becomes:
choices: Four times as long.
One quarter.
Unchanged.
questions.hint: Use timescale ≈ available energy / luminosity.
questions.feedback: With the same energy reservoir and four times the rate of release, the approximate timescale is divided by four.

questions.prompt: A star starts at 30 M☉, loses 8 M☉ in winds, then transfers 4 M☉ to its companion. Its remaining mass in this accounting toy model is:
questions.hint: Subtract both mass-loss channels from the initial mass.
questions.feedback: 30−8−4=18 M☉; real binary mass changes can also involve accretion and additional outflows.

objectives.title: Trace metallicity and wind effects
objectives.evidence: Explain conditional effects of line-driven winds and why metallicity is not a deterministic remnant label.

questions.prompt: Under otherwise comparable massive-star conditions, lower metallicity often weakens which mass-loss channel?
choices: Gravitational-wave emission from a single noncompact star.
Metal-line-driven stellar winds.
The definition of initial binary separation.
questions.hint: Recall that metallic absorption lines transfer radiative momentum to outer layers.
questions.feedback: Fewer heavy-element line absorbers often reduce line-driven wind efficiency, leaving more stellar mass available for later evolution under a specified model.

questions.prompt: Why is 'low metallicity guarantees a heavier black hole' too strong?
choices: Metallicity does not influence any wind model.
Binary interactions, rotation, explosion prescriptions and other mass-loss channels also influence the final remnant.
Every low-metallicity massive star collapses directly into a black hole of its birth mass.
questions.hint: Look for multiple evolutionary mechanisms affecting the final core and envelope.
questions.feedback: Metallicity can affect wind mass loss, but outcomes depend on initial mass, binary interaction, remnant prescriptions and other assumptions.

questions.prompt: Why must a population model track star-formation metallicity rather than only present-day metallicity?
choices: Every star changes its birth metallicity to the current cosmic mean.
Progenitors formed earlier under the metallicity distribution at their formation epoch.
Gravitational waves directly measure the host's birth metallicity without inference.
questions.hint: Merger time can be long after the binary formed.
questions.feedback: Compact binaries encode delayed stellar histories; their birth metallicity distribution can differ from the environment at merger time.

objectives.title: Critique stellar-to-remnant inference
objectives.evidence: Separate an observable, a simulation prescription and an uncertain inferred physical outcome.

questions.prompt: Two simulations give different black-hole masses from the same zero-age mass. What should be checked first?
choices: Which output filename is shorter.
Wind, mixing, binary-interaction and remnant-formation prescriptions.
Whether both simulations obey identical black-hole mass distributions by definition.
questions.hint: Compare assumptions and evolutionary histories, not just their final scalar output.
questions.feedback: Massive-star evolution depends on multiple prescriptions; differences do not alone identify which code or physics is correct.

questions.prompt: Can one infer a star's full evolution uniquely from one point on an H–R diagram?
choices: Yes; temperature and luminosity fix all historical parameters exactly.
No; multiple masses, ages and evolutionary tracks can occupy similar locations.
Only if distance is measured to the nearest metre.
questions.hint: Consider age, composition, extinction and binary contamination.
questions.feedback: Luminosity and temperature are useful constraints but do not generally identify a unique evolutionary history.

questions.prompt: A toy calculation assigns every massive star the same wind mass loss independent of composition. What scientific question does it fail to explore?
choices: The number of rows in an output table.
Sensitivity of final masses to metallicity-dependent wind prescriptions.
Whether all stars have identical initial masses.
questions.hint: Ask which physical variable the prescription deliberately ignores.
questions.feedback: Holding mass loss constant across metallicity removes that pathway from the model and cannot test its impact on remnant populations.

cases.title: Two birth environments
cases.scenario: Two otherwise comparable toy massive stars start at 35 M☉. Model A loses 15 M☉ in winds and Model B loses 5 M☉.
cases.task: Calculate pre-collapse masses and explain why final remnant masses still cannot be read off directly.
steps: A has 20 M☉ remaining and B has 30 M☉ remaining.
Wind mass loss changes the pre-collapse budget.
Explosion, fallback, binary interaction and remnant prescription are unprovided.
cases.solution: The model suggests a possible effect of wind prescriptions, not a one-to-one black-hole mass prediction.

cases.title: Observed hot star
cases.scenario: An H–R diagram places a hot luminous star near two model tracks with different mass and binary histories.
cases.task: List evidence needed before assigning a unique progenitor path.
steps: Check observational uncertainties in luminosity/temperature and distance/extinction.
Inspect metallicity, rotation and possible binary contamination.
Compare multiple evolutionary tracks and quantify model uncertainty.
cases.solution: A single location in an H–R diagram constrains, but does not by itself uniquely reconstruct, stellar history.

sources.title: The Evolution of Massive Binary Stars (review)

sets.title: Roche geometry and mass-transfer stability
sets.summary: Distinguish overflow onset, transfer rate, stability response and angular-momentum changes.

objectives.title: Identify when transfer begins
objectives.evidence: Connect Roche-lobe filling with binary separation and the donor's radius.

questions.prompt: What is the usual geometric trigger for Roche-lobe overflow in a binary model?
choices: The companion's radius must be exactly zero.
The donor expands to fill or overfill its Roche lobe.
The binary must first become unbound.
questions.hint: Compare donor radius with its effective Roche-lobe radius.
questions.feedback: Roche-lobe overflow begins when the donor fills its effective equipotential boundary, allowing material to pass toward its companion.

questions.prompt: Does filling a Roche lobe alone determine whether mass transfer is dynamically stable?
choices: Yes; all overflowing donors transfer stably forever.
No; compare how donor radius and Roche-lobe radius respond to mass loss.
Yes; every overflowing donor instantly enters a common envelope.
questions.hint: Onset geometry and dynamical stability are separate questions.
questions.feedback: Stability depends on structural response, orbital evolution, mass ratio and timescale, not on geometry alone.

questions.prompt: In the usual binary-star terminology, the donor is:
choices: Always the initially less massive star.
The star losing mass to the other component or out of the system.
The remnant formed at the end of every binary simulation.
questions.hint: Define the direction of mass exchange at the current episode.
questions.feedback: Donor and accretor identify instantaneous mass-transfer roles; roles may change in complex histories.

objectives.title: Calculate mass and orbit budgets
objectives.evidence: Apply simple conservative-transfer accounting before considering non-conservative loss.

questions.prompt: In a conservative transfer episode, donor mass drops from 10 to 8 M☉ and the companion began at 6 M☉. The companion ends at:
questions.hint: Mass lost by the donor is gained by the companion if the system loses none.
questions.feedback: The donor loses 2 M☉, so the accretor gains 2 M☉ and ends at 8 M☉.

questions.prompt: A donor loses 3 M☉; the companion gains 1 M☉. With no other mass changes, how much leaves the binary?
questions.hint: Subtract accreted material from donor mass loss.
questions.feedback: The remaining 2 M☉ leaves the modeled binary; this is non-conservative mass transfer.

questions.prompt: A 12 M☉ donor transfers 4 M☉ conservatively to a 5 M☉ companion. The final donor-to-accretor mass ratio is:
questions.hint: Update both masses before taking their ratio.
questions.feedback: The donor ends at 8 M☉ and companion at 9 M☉, so q=8/9 under this toy accounting.

objectives.title: Reason about stability and feedback
objectives.evidence: Compare donor shrinkage/expansion with Roche-lobe change and timescale.

questions.prompt: Suppose mass loss causes the donor to expand faster than its Roche lobe. What feedback can occur?
choices: Overflow necessarily stops immediately.
Overfilling grows and mass transfer can run away.
The Roche lobe ceases to exist.
questions.hint: Compare the two evolving radii rather than a fixed-radius snapshot.
questions.feedback: If donor radius increases relative to the Roche boundary, overflow deepens; the resulting runaway can occur on short timescales, depending on the model.

questions.prompt: Why can a convective-envelope giant be more vulnerable to unstable transfer in some mass-ratio regimes?
choices: Convective envelopes guarantee conservative transfer.
Its structural radius response to mass loss can worsen overflow.
Convection prevents all Roche-lobe overflow.
questions.hint: Think about the donor's response to rapid stripping.
questions.feedback: A donor's adiabatic radius response and the Roche-lobe response govern stability; extended convective giants can expand under rapid mass loss in relevant regimes.

questions.prompt: A binary changes its mass ratio during transfer. Why may the orbit's evolution change sign?
choices: The orbit has a fixed direction of change independent of initial masses.
Mass transfer redistributes masses and angular momentum; the orbital response depends on their evolving values.
Mass ratio cannot change during transfer.
questions.hint: Track the component masses and any angular momentum carried away.
questions.feedback: Conservative transfer and non-conservative outflows can shrink or widen an orbit under different mass ratios and angular-momentum prescriptions.

objectives.title: Inspect assumptions in a transfer model
objectives.evidence: Identify missing angular momentum, timescale or accretion efficiency assumptions.

questions.prompt: A simulation says 'stable transfer' but gives only the initial mass ratio. What else is needed to evaluate this claim?
choices: Only the initial component labels.
Donor evolutionary state, response to mass loss and Roche-lobe/orbital prescription.
A detector noise spectrum at merger.
questions.hint: Stability thresholds depend on stellar structure and response, not just q.
questions.feedback: Mass ratio is one input; stellar-envelope structure, timescales, accretion and angular-momentum loss can affect the stability criterion.

questions.prompt: A model assumes fully conservative transfer but its reported total binary mass decreases with no other process. What is the immediate issue?
choices: The star-formation history is always wrong.
Mass accounting contradicts the stated assumption.
Conservative transfer requires the donor and accretor to have equal mass.
questions.hint: Total mass is fixed during the idealized conservative transfer episode.
questions.feedback: Under genuinely conservative transfer with no other process, the donor's lost mass should equal the companion's gain.

questions.prompt: Two models predict different post-transfer separations. Which comparison can isolate the effect of angular-momentum loss?
choices: Change winds, kicks, transfer efficiency and initial binaries simultaneously.
Hold other assumptions fixed and vary the outflow's specific-angular-momentum prescription.
Ignore separation and compare only model names.
questions.hint: Use one-change-at-a-time sensitivity checks where possible.
questions.feedback: Changing multiple inputs at once confounds the physical cause; controlled model comparisons clarify parameter sensitivity.

cases.title: Mass-transfer ledger
cases.scenario: A 14 M☉ donor loses 5 M☉; a 9 M☉ companion accretes 3 M☉; all other changes are neglected.
cases.task: Compute final masses, mass lost to the surroundings and whether the episode is conservative.
steps: Donor: 14−5=9 M☉.
Companion: 9+3=12 M☉.
2 M☉ was not accreted and is lost to the surroundings.
cases.solution: The binary total decreases from 23 to 21 M☉; this is non-conservative transfer and its orbital impact additionally needs the angular momentum carried by escaping matter.

cases.title: Geometry versus stability
cases.scenario: A donor just fills its Roche lobe. A model predicts that after small mass loss its radius increases by 3% but its Roche radius increases by 1%.
cases.task: Predict the qualitative overflow response and name missing information.
steps: Donor radius grows relative to its Roche boundary.
Overflow therefore deepens in this local comparison.
Further stability analysis needs the response over appropriate timescales and the mass-transfer prescription.
cases.solution: The local response suggests positive feedback; it does not uniquely establish the eventual outcome from one step alone.

sources.title: The Evolution of Massive Binary Stars (review)

sets.title: Common-envelope energetics and channels
sets.summary: Test drag, envelope binding, efficiency assumptions and why short-period survivors matter.

objectives.title: Describe the interaction
objectives.evidence: Distinguish common-envelope evolution from ordinary stable transfer.

questions.prompt: A common-envelope episode usually involves:
choices: Two unrelated stars separated by many parsecs.
A companion moving within a shared stellar envelope while drag exchanges orbital energy and angular momentum with gas.
A stable empty cavity that cannot exchange energy.
questions.hint: Look for the phase involving an envelope shared with the companion.
questions.feedback: Envelope gas can drain orbital energy and angular momentum, potentially ejecting gas and dramatically tightening the binary.

questions.prompt: Does a common-envelope episode necessarily end with two surviving compact remnants?
choices: Yes; every episode produces two black holes immediately.
No; the binary may merge during the envelope phase or emerge as a tighter noncompact/compact pair.
Yes; envelope ejection is guaranteed if the donor fills its lobe.
questions.hint: Consider ejection versus in-envelope merger and later stellar evolution.
questions.feedback: CE outcomes depend on envelope binding, energy transfer and stellar structure; any later compact-object formation is a separate evolutionary step.

questions.prompt: Which feature often motivates a common-envelope phase in compact-binary formation models?
choices: It turns the system into a three-body orbit by definition.
It can reduce orbital separation enough to enable a later merger within a cosmic time.
It removes the need for any subsequent supernova or remnant evolution.
questions.hint: Think about long inspiral times at large separation.
questions.feedback: Orbital tightening in some surviving systems can greatly shorten eventual gravitational-wave inspiral times.

objectives.title: Apply a simplified energy budget
objectives.evidence: Distinguish released orbital-energy magnitude from ejection efficiency and binding energy.

questions.prompt: In a toy energy formalism, an envelope needs 6 energy units to unbind and the usable fraction of released orbital energy is 0.5. What released energy is needed if no other source contributes?
choices: 3 units.
12 units.
6.5 units.
questions.hint: Solve α ΔE_release≥E_bind for ΔE_release.
questions.feedback: At efficiency α=0.5, at least 6/0.5=12 released-energy units are required under the model.

questions.prompt: If a binary's orbital energy changes from −4 to −10 units during shrinkage, the orbital energy released in magnitude is:
choices: −14 units.
6 units.
14 units.
questions.hint: Released energy is the drop in orbital energy magnitude: E_initial−E_final.
questions.feedback: The orbital energy decreases by 6 units, releasing 6 units to other degrees of freedom in this simplified account.

questions.prompt: A toy envelope's binding energy magnitude doubles at unchanged available released orbital energy and α. Ejection in the same energy-budget model becomes:
choices: Guaranteed to be easier.
More difficult.
Unaffected by binding energy.
questions.hint: Compare required energy with accessible energy.
questions.feedback: Doubling the required energy while holding supply fixed makes the toy inequality α ΔE_release≥E_bind harder to satisfy.

objectives.title: Trace orbital shrinkage and outcomes
objectives.evidence: Connect drag, available energy and post-envelope binary evolution.

questions.prompt: What is a direct channel by which an embedded companion can lose orbital energy?
choices: A compulsory increase in the companion's rest mass.
Dynamical interaction and drag with surrounding envelope gas.
The instantaneous absence of any force.
questions.hint: The envelope is not dynamically inert.
questions.feedback: The companion's motion through gas excites flows and transfers orbital energy and angular momentum into the envelope.

questions.prompt: If the envelope is ejected before the cores merge, the remnant binary is commonly:
choices: Forced to have exactly its initial separation.
Much more compact than before the interaction.
Always a pair of already formed black holes.
questions.hint: Think about the energy source used to help eject gas.
questions.feedback: Shrinking orbital separation can release orbital energy and leave a closer pair of stellar cores/remnants; later evolution is model-dependent.

questions.prompt: Why can stronger assumed envelope binding increase predicted merger-within-envelope outcomes?
choices: More binding energy guarantees that the envelope escapes spontaneously.
More orbital energy must be transferred before ejection, potentially requiring a smaller separation than survival allows.
Envelope binding energy is unrelated to any ejection model.
questions.hint: Think about competition between envelope ejection and core coalescence.
questions.feedback: In a simple budget, a more tightly bound envelope needs more accessible energy; the companion may spiral in too far before successful ejection.

objectives.title: Critique an efficiency prescription
objectives.evidence: Recognize that an energy parameter is an approximation rather than a directly observed universal constant.

questions.prompt: A model claims that a single chosen CE efficiency parameter is a measured universal constant for all stellar envelopes. What is the concern?
choices: The common-envelope concept cannot be modeled numerically.
The parameter is a simplified and uncertain prescription that may vary with system properties.
Efficiency automatically equals the donor-to-companion mass ratio.
questions.hint: Separate parameterized modeling from universal measurement.
questions.feedback: CE evolution is multidimensional and uncertain; one energy-efficiency parameter is not established as a universal measured constant.

questions.prompt: Can successful energy-budget ejection alone prove a realistic post-envelope binary survives?
choices: Yes; a positive energy budget guarantees no core collision.
No; final core radii, orbital separation and merger conditions also need checking.
No; conservation of energy is invalid for any binary.
questions.hint: Satisfying a necessary toy inequality may not be sufficient for physical survival.
questions.feedback: A model must also check whether the post-spiral-in separation accommodates the surviving objects and whether other losses occur.

questions.prompt: What should accompany a comparison of predicted merger rates under two CE prescriptions?
choices: Only the higher rate with no uncertainties.
A statement of the changed parameters and which other binary and cosmic assumptions were held fixed.
A claim that both outputs are direct measurements of the real Universe.
questions.hint: Rates mix binary-physics assumptions with population weighting and cosmic history.
questions.feedback: Documenting assumptions and controlled variations is essential to interpret an uncertain evolutionary pathway.

cases.title: Envelope energy audit
cases.scenario: A toy CE event has |E_bind|=10 units, ΔE_release=15 units and α=0.6, with no other energy source.
cases.task: Does the elementary budget predict enough usable energy for ejection, and what does it not establish?
steps: Available useful energy =0.6×15=9 units.
9<10, so this toy budget does not reach the required envelope binding energy.
Other physical energy sources and hydrodynamic outcomes are outside the simplified model.
cases.solution: The simple α-energy budget fails its ejection inequality; this alone cannot establish the physical result of a complete hydrodynamic CE simulation.

cases.title: Outcome dependence
cases.scenario: Two models use the same pre-CE binary but assign different donor envelope binding energies.
cases.task: State a controlled comparison and two outcomes to track.
steps: Hold initial masses, separation and other prescriptions fixed.
Vary only binding-energy evaluation or efficiency.
Record ejected envelope versus core merger and surviving post-CE separation.
cases.solution: The experiment identifies sensitivity to CE energetics without claiming that one prescription is observationally proven.

sources.title: The Evolution of Massive Binary Stars (review)

sets.title: Compact remnants and formation channels
sets.summary: Trace core-collapse outcomes, supernova mass loss, natal kicks and the formation of merging compact-object binaries.

objectives.title: Distinguish remnant pathways
objectives.evidence: Explain the meanings of compact remnant, neutron star and black hole without a deterministic birth-mass threshold.

questions.prompt: Which objects are commonly called stellar compact remnants?
choices: Only galaxies and dark-matter haloes.
White dwarfs, neutron stars and stellar-origin black holes.
Only planets and main-sequence stars.
questions.hint: Distinguish stellar endpoints supported by degeneracy pressure or gravitational collapse.
questions.feedback: Compact remnants include white dwarfs, neutron stars and black holes; the exact pathway depends on progenitor and interaction history.

questions.prompt: Does every star above one universal birth-mass threshold produce an identical black-hole mass?
choices: Yes; all stars collapse at the same age and composition.
No; metallicity, winds, binary interaction and remnant-formation prescriptions matter.
Yes; remnant mass is exactly equal to initial mass.
questions.hint: Follow the mass retained in the core and envelope rather than using only initial mass.
questions.feedback: No single deterministic mass mapping describes all evolutionary channels; even toy prescriptions must state their assumptions.

questions.prompt: Why is a double compact-object binary not automatically a future observable gravitational-wave merger?
choices: Gravitational waves exist only from a single compact body.
Its separation, eccentricity, evolution and inspiral time may prevent a merger within the relevant time window.
Every compact pair merges instantly upon formation.
questions.hint: Formation, merger and detection are different stages.
questions.feedback: A bound double compact object can have an inspiral time exceeding the age of the Universe or lie outside instrumental sensitivity.

objectives.title: Calculate simplified formation budgets
objectives.evidence: Use mass, velocity and delay-time accounting in toy remnant histories.

questions.prompt: A 9 M☉ pre-collapse star leaves a 1.5 M☉ compact remnant in a toy model. How much mass is ejected?
questions.hint: Subtract retained remnant mass from pre-event stellar mass.
questions.feedback: 9−1.5=7.5 M☉ ejected; this toy ledger does not specify asymmetry or kinetic-energy distribution.

questions.prompt: A remnant has pre-event velocity (+70,0) km/s and receives kick (0,+24) km/s. Its new speed is:
choices: 46 km/s.
74 km/s.
94 km/s.
questions.hint: Add perpendicular velocity components and use the Pythagorean theorem.
questions.feedback: sqrt(70²+24²)=sqrt(5476)=74 km/s; the vector is (+70,+24) km/s.

questions.prompt: A compact binary forms 2 Gyr after star formation and merges another 5 Gyr later. What is its total formation-to-merger delay?
choices: 10 Gyr.
7 Gyr.
3 Gyr.
questions.hint: Distinguish stellar evolution time from the compact-binary inspiral time.
questions.feedback: 2+5=7 Gyr from initial star formation to merger; some population models use a different explicitly stated delay definition.

objectives.title: Explain disruptions and surviving channels
objectives.evidence: Distinguish mass-loss and kick mechanisms in a specified binary frame.

questions.prompt: Why can a rapid supernova disrupt a previously bound binary?
choices: The binary is guaranteed to keep its exact orbital energy.
Mass loss can reduce binding gravity while a kick changes the relative orbital velocity.
The presence of any neutron star makes gravity repulsive.
questions.hint: Write post-event ε=v_rel²/2−GM_after/r.
questions.feedback: The gravitational mass and instantaneous relative velocity can both change, altering the orbit's specific energy and survival.

questions.prompt: Two otherwise identical compact-binary progenitors have different post-event orbital separations. Why might their merger times differ substantially?
choices: Orbital separation matters only to optical brightness.
Under circular point-mass GW evolution, inspiral time scales strongly with separation (as a⁴ for fixed masses).
Merger time is completely independent of initial separation.
questions.hint: Recall the steep separation dependence of GW-driven inspiral.
questions.feedback: For fixed component masses and circular orbits, a factor of two in separation corresponds to a factor of sixteen in idealized inspiral time.

questions.prompt: How can an isolated-binary formation path differ from a dynamical formation path?
choices: An isolated path necessarily includes an encounter with a third black hole.
One evolves from a pre-existing stellar binary, while the other can assemble or exchange members through many-body encounters.
A dynamical path forbids all gravitational forces.
questions.hint: Look at what brings the two compact objects into a pair.
questions.feedback: Field binary interactions versus dense-environment encounters can lead to different distributions of masses, spins, eccentricities and delays under particular models.

objectives.title: Qualify population-level remnant conclusions
objectives.evidence: Recognize uncertain kick, mass-loss and explosion prescriptions and distinguish intrinsic from observed populations.

questions.prompt: A simulated black-hole mass spectrum disagrees with detections. Which conclusion follows immediately?
choices: Observed detections are an unbiased draw of all births.
The combination of formation, cosmic history, selection and measurement assumptions needs investigation.
A single remnant mass prescription is proven wrong by definition.
questions.hint: An observed sample is filtered by several physical and statistical processes.
questions.feedback: One mismatch does not isolate which physical prescription or selection model is responsible.

questions.prompt: A remnant model predicts zero natal kicks for every black hole. What should a research report call this?
choices: A direct consequence of Newton's first law.
An explicit modeling assumption whose sensitivity should be tested.
A universally measured property of every black hole.
questions.hint: Distinguish a prescription from an established measurement.
questions.feedback: Zero-kick prescriptions can be useful scenarios, but their population predictions should be compared with alternative kick assumptions.

questions.prompt: Can a detected gravitational-wave mass be equated without caveat to a progenitor's zero-age main-sequence mass?
choices: Yes; detector strain directly measures initial stellar radius.
No; stellar evolution, binary interactions and gravitational-wave parameter inference separate the two.
Yes; initial and measured final masses are identical by conservation of mass.
questions.hint: Track formation history and uncertainty between progenitor and merger.
questions.feedback: Detector inference concerns compact-object merger parameters; inferring birth masses is a model-dependent inverse problem.

cases.title: Survival versus future merger
cases.scenario: Two compact-binary models give circular separations a and 2a at fixed masses, ignoring subsequent environmental effects.
cases.task: Compare idealized GW inspiral times and explain what a survival check alone misses.
steps: Peters-type circular inspiral time scales as a⁴ for fixed masses.
The wider binary takes 2⁴=16 times longer.
Both binaries may be bound but only one might merge within an observational time window.
cases.solution: Binding at formation and merging within a specified horizon are separate filters on a simulated population.

cases.title: Mass ledger and kick
cases.scenario: A toy 10 M☉ star leaves a 2 M☉ remnant; its pre-event velocity is (+100,0) km/s and its kick is (−20,+60) km/s.
cases.task: Find the ejected mass and final velocity, then explain why binary survival remains unknown.
steps: Ejected mass=10−2=8 M☉.
Final velocity=(80,60) km/s with speed 100 km/s.
Companion mass, instantaneous separation and post-event relative motion are missing.
cases.solution: The final speed alone cannot decide survival; mass loss and relative orbital energy must be computed.

sets.title: Gravitational-wave generation and chirps
sets.summary: Reason about quadrupole radiation, chirp mass, frequency evolution and detector/source-frame interpretation.

objectives.title: Connect motion to emitted waves
objectives.evidence: Explain time-varying mass quadrupoles, wave strain and inspiral-merger-ringdown.

questions.prompt: At leading order, what source property generates gravitational radiation in the weak-field slow-motion approximation?
choices: A constant total mass with no changing multipole moments.
A time-varying mass quadrupole moment.
Any static isolated spherical mass.
questions.hint: Remember the leading radiative multipole for gravity.
questions.feedback: The leading far-field signal involves time derivatives of the mass quadrupole; stationary spherical distributions do not radiate at this order.

questions.prompt: What does dimensionless interferometer gravitational-wave strain h represent?
choices: The source's mass in kilograms.
A fractional differential change in the detector's arm lengths in an idealized response description.
The absolute number of photons detected per second.
questions.hint: Relate the wave to fractional stretching/squeezing of separations.
questions.feedback: Strain is dimensionless and is related to relative length change; real detector calibration and antenna response must also be considered.

questions.prompt: In the common compact-binary waveform sequence, the 'ringdown' refers to:
choices: A detector's yearly mirror replacement.
Damped oscillations of the remnant after merger.
Steady hydrogen fusion before the stars are born.
questions.hint: Think of perturbations of the post-merger compact remnant.
questions.feedback: A settling remnant emits damped modes; the waveform before merger includes inspiral and strong-field merger dynamics.

objectives.title: Compute chirp-mass and period scalings
objectives.evidence: Use the definition M_c=(m₁m₂)^(3/5)/(m₁+m₂)^(1/5) and simple circular-binary scalings.

questions.prompt: For an equal-mass binary m₁=m₂=m, the chirp mass is:
questions.hint: Insert m₁=m₂=m into the chirp-mass expression.

questions.prompt: A quasi-circular binary has orbital frequency 50 Hz. Its dominant quadrupole GW frequency is approximately:
choices: 50 Hz.
25 Hz.
questions.hint: The leading quadrupole varies twice per orbital cycle.
questions.feedback: For the dominant (l,m)=(2,2) mode of a quasi-circular binary, f_GW≈2 f_orb.

questions.prompt: In a toy leading-order inspiral with fixed masses, GW frequency increases over time. The observed cycle spacing in a time trace:
choices: Stays constant.
Decreases.
Increases without limit.
questions.hint: Frequency is the reciprocal of period.
questions.feedback: As f increases, the period 1/f decreases: successive cycles arrive closer together, producing the 'chirp'.

objectives.title: Explain waveform evolution
objectives.evidence: Relate radiation of energy/angular momentum to tighter orbit and higher characteristic frequency.

questions.prompt: Why does the leading-order orbital frequency rise during a compact-binary inspiral?
choices: An inspiral requires its component masses to increase at every orbit.
Gravitational radiation removes orbital energy and angular momentum, shrinking the orbit.
Waves supply the binary with unlimited positive orbital energy.
questions.hint: Connect loss of orbital energy with separation and Kepler's law.
questions.feedback: For an isolated quasi-circular compact binary, GW emission tightens the orbit and drives faster orbital motion until the approximations fail near merger.

questions.prompt: At the same intrinsic chirp mass and source evolution, a more distant source generally has:
choices: Exactly equal detector strain independent of orientation.
Smaller detected strain amplitude, all else equal.
Larger strain because light travels longer.
questions.hint: Think of wave amplitude fall-off plus orientation/antenna factors.
questions.feedback: At leading order amplitude scales inversely with distance, but actual observed strain also depends on inclination, polarization and detector response.

questions.prompt: Why does a nonzero source redshift alter mass interpretation from observed detector-frame waveform timescales?
choices: Redshift changes only photon brightness, never GW frequency.
Observed waveform timescales are stretched by (1+z), producing a detector-frame mass scale (1+z) times source-frame mass.
The source's rest mass grows physically during propagation.
questions.hint: Cosmological redshift stretches observed periods for gravitational waves too.
questions.feedback: At cosmological distances, the waveform naturally constrains redshifted mass parameters; source-frame masses require redshift information or a distance–cosmology relation.

objectives.title: Distinguish approximations and inference
objectives.evidence: Identify regime limitations, degeneracies and why detector strain is not a direct progenitor record.

questions.prompt: When might a leading-order circular point-mass inspiral formula be inadequate?
choices: Only when a detector is offline.
Near merger or for important spin, eccentricity, tidal or strong-field effects.
Whenever two compact objects are bound.
questions.hint: Ask what the low-velocity weak-field assumptions omit.
questions.feedback: Reliable inference near merger requires more complete waveform models; spin, eccentricity, tides and instrument response may affect the signal.

questions.prompt: Does a measured chirp mass by itself uniquely determine both component masses?
choices: No; chirp mass has no connection to component masses.
No; many mass pairs can share a chirp mass without additional information.
Yes; one scalar fixes two independent masses uniquely.
questions.hint: Count parameters compared with independent constraints.
questions.feedback: Additional waveform features help constrain mass ratio/spins; chirp mass alone is insufficient to identify each component mass.

questions.prompt: A waveform fit constrains merger component masses. What extra step is needed to claim a particular stellar formation channel?
choices: Assume every compact binary came from one channel.
Compare predictions of competing formation models after accounting for cosmic history, selection and parameter uncertainty.
Read the progenitor's birthplace directly from the strain time series.
questions.hint: Separate the inverse problem of formation history from a compact-binary parameter fit.
questions.feedback: Different formation histories can predict overlapping merger properties; population-level modeling and uncertainty are necessary.

cases.title: Equal-mass chirp
cases.scenario: Two equal-mass objects each have m=10 M☉ in an idealized system.
cases.task: Calculate chirp mass numerically to two significant digits; name an inference the result cannot make.
steps: For equal masses M_c=m/2^(1/5).
Chirp mass alone does not determine formation channel or source redshift.
cases.solution: About 8.7 M☉ in the specified frame. Additional waveform parameters, distance and population models are needed for broader claims.

cases.title: Detector-frame scaling
cases.scenario: An illustrative source has source-frame chirp mass 20 M☉ and redshift z=0.5.
cases.task: Compute its detector-frame chirp mass and state what the mass conversion assumes.
steps: M_c,det=(1+z) M_c,src.
This uses the cosmological redshift relation; independent z information or a cosmological model is needed to recover source masses.
cases.solution: The detector-frame chirp mass is 30 M☉; redshifted time/frequency scales should not be interpreted as a physical increase in source rest mass.

sets.title: Interferometers, noise and evidence
sets.summary: Separate detector response, signal-to-noise, noise transients, networks and selection limitations.

objectives.title: Interpret a detector response
objectives.evidence: Describe differential arm response and distinguish signal from local instrumental noise.

questions.prompt: Why do laser interferometers compare two arm lengths?
choices: Every equal-arm noise fluctuation is a new astrophysical source.
A passing gravitational wave can produce a time-varying differential arm-length signal.
The two arms measure the black hole's radius directly.
questions.hint: Think of relative stretching of orthogonal directions.
questions.feedback: Differential arm readout is sensitive to GW strain projected onto detector geometry; instrumental disturbances can also affect this channel.

questions.prompt: Why is one strong transient in a single interferometer not automatically proof of an astrophysical merger?
choices: A real GW only affects one detector by definition.
Instrumental glitches and terrestrial noise can imitate signal-like transients.
Every large strain fluctuation must be a GW.
questions.hint: Think about comparing coherence across detectors and modeling noise.
questions.feedback: Multi-detector coincidence, waveform consistency and background estimation help distinguish astrophysical signals from instrumental artefacts.

questions.prompt: What is the main advantage of observing a signal in detectors with different orientations and locations?
choices: Detector separation eliminates all calibration uncertainty.
Coherent time/phase/amplitude information can strengthen interpretation and constrain sky position and polarization.
All detectors always record exactly equal wave amplitudes.
questions.hint: Compare travel-time delays and antenna responses.
questions.feedback: A geographically distributed network samples the wave differently and can improve localization and consistency tests.

objectives.title: Compute response and SNR toy quantities
objectives.evidence: Reason with h≈ΔL/L and noise-weighted detection metrics without treating them as complete pipelines.

questions.prompt: A toy interferometer has an arm length of 4000 m and an idealized fractional strain h=10⁻²¹. The associated scale hL is:
questions.hint: Multiply dimensionless strain by length; this ignores antenna and optical response factors.
questions.feedback: 4000×10⁻²¹=4×10⁻¹⁸ m. Real instruments infer differential strain through calibrated optical responses.

questions.prompt: If the same signal amplitude is observed against twice the noise-amplitude spectral density in a comparable toy frequency band, its approximate amplitude SNR:
choices: Stays exactly unchanged for every possible noise shape.
Halves.
Doubles.
questions.hint: SNR measures signal against noise after appropriate weighting.
questions.feedback: At fixed signal and identical spectral shape, doubling noise amplitude approximately halves matched-filter SNR; broadband results need integration.

questions.prompt: Two interferometers see coherent arrival times 7 ms apart. Can that delay alone uniquely fix the source's exact sky position?
choices: No; gravitational waves always arrive everywhere simultaneously.
No; a time delay defines a locus of possible directions, with additional information needed.
Yes; two time measurements fix all sky coordinates uniquely.
questions.hint: Geometric time-delay constraints are not a unique full-sky localization.
questions.feedback: Timing provides a projected-baseline constraint; amplitude, phase and more detectors improve localization.

objectives.title: Explain false alarms and sensitivity
objectives.evidence: Reason how background, antenna orientation and observation time change the detected sample.

questions.prompt: Why is a detector's reported detection threshold not simply a universal intrinsic black-hole mass cutoff?
choices: Detector noise depends only on progenitor metallicity.
Sensitivity depends on waveform masses/spins, distance, orientation, noise and search method.
All binaries with masses above a threshold are observed regardless of distance.
questions.hint: Consider source amplitude and the instrument/search response.
questions.feedback: A detector samples a selection function over source parameters and conditions; one fixed mass alone does not determine detectability.

questions.prompt: What changes when detector noise worsens during a run, with the same source population?
choices: Every source's intrinsic mass doubles.
The detection efficiency for otherwise identical signals can decrease.
The physical cosmic merger rate instantly decreases.
questions.hint: Separate detector sensitivity from astrophysical event production.
questions.feedback: Higher noise generally reduces SNR and can reduce detection probability; it does not alter the underlying astrophysical birth or merger rate.

questions.prompt: Why is a noise-background estimate needed when claiming a detection?
choices: Background estimation proves a formation channel uniquely.
Search statistics can also arise from non-astrophysical fluctuations, so significance needs a false-alarm model.
A noise model is only necessary after publishing an event.
questions.hint: Distinguish signal consistency from the frequency of noise mimics.
questions.feedback: A candidate's ranking statistic needs context from the search background; this is separate from astrophysical population inference.

objectives.title: Critique observational interpretation
objectives.evidence: Distinguish physical source properties, detector-frame parameters and instrument/calibration uncertainties.

questions.prompt: Can a non-detection of one predicted binary prove it did not exist?
choices: Only if its host galaxy is optically invisible.
No; it may have been too distant, unfavorably oriented, outside a sensitive band or during downtime.
Yes; all astrophysical binaries are detected.
questions.hint: Distinguish source existence from the probability that it is recorded.
questions.feedback: Non-detection constrains populations through the detection efficiency and observing time, not a single source's existence in general.

questions.prompt: A claimed population shift is based on detections from two observing runs with different sensitivities. What should be compared before attributing it to astrophysics?
choices: Whether the data filenames match.
Run-dependent selection functions, pipelines and measurement uncertainties.
Only the raw number of observed waveforms.
questions.hint: Detector improvements change which part of the population is visible.
questions.feedback: Apparent distribution differences can result from changing instruments and analysis rather than evolving astrophysical populations.

questions.prompt: Why does a network-calibrated event not uniquely reveal the host galaxy in most cases?
choices: Every detected binary has an electromagnetic counterpart.
Sky localization and distance are uncertain, and multiple galaxies may lie in the allowed volume.
An interferometer reads galaxy names as electromagnetic signals.
questions.hint: Think about broad positional and distance posteriors.
questions.feedback: GW parameter estimation often yields a three-dimensional localization volume rather than a unique host identification.

cases.title: Strain scale
cases.scenario: A toy strain of 2×10⁻²¹ acts on a 4 km arm. Treat ΔL≈hL only for an order-of-magnitude illustration.
cases.task: Calculate ΔL, then name two detector factors not represented.
steps: Convert 4 km to 4000 m.
Antenna response, optical transfer, noise and calibration affect real measurements.
cases.solution: An order-of-magnitude length scale is 8×10⁻¹⁸ m, not a universal measured displacement of one mirror.

cases.title: Candidate comparison
cases.scenario: A hypothetical candidate appears in two detectors with arrival times consistent with light travel, but one detector also reports a large environmental disturbance.
cases.task: What must be checked before interpreting the pair as an astrophysical GW?
steps: Inspect detector state and environmental/instrumental vetoes.
Check coherent waveform consistency and background false-alarm estimation.
Account for calibration and the second detector's signal strength.
cases.solution: Coincidence is useful evidence but alone cannot replace an instrument-quality and noise-background analysis.

sets.title: Population synthesis and Monte Carlo sampling
sets.summary: Connect sampled initial conditions, binary histories, statistical weights and sensitivity checks.

objectives.title: Read a population model
objectives.evidence: Distinguish simulated systems, birth distributions, evolution prescriptions and observable samples.

questions.prompt: What does a rapid binary-population synthesis model typically evolve?
choices: A single galaxy's exact future without uncertainty.
Many sampled initial binary systems under prescribed stellar and binary physics.
Only one observed gravitational waveform with no stellar history.
questions.hint: Identify the input ensemble and evolution rules.
questions.feedback: Population synthesis maps assumed birth conditions through approximated stellar/binary evolution to distributions of outcomes.

questions.prompt: Why might a simulated binary produce more than one row in an event log?
choices: A binary is forbidden from experiencing more than one mass-transfer event.
The same system can undergo multiple recorded phases or events.
Every row must correspond to an independently born binary.
questions.hint: Separate the unit of sampling from the unit of recorded events.
questions.feedback: One system can have repeated mass transfers or supernovae, so event rows are not independent system counts.

questions.prompt: What is a formation efficiency in a specified population-synthesis model?
choices: An instrument's noise floor in strain per root hertz.
The yield of a defined class of outcomes per appropriately normalized formed stellar mass or comparable stated birth normalization.
The percentage of rows with nonempty filenames.
questions.hint: Always state the denominator and outcome definition.
questions.feedback: Formation efficiencies require a defined mass/initial-population normalization and a defined event class; choices influence interpretation.

objectives.title: Compute weighted counts and uncertainty
objectives.evidence: Distinguish raw counts from sums of sampling weights and estimate toy sampling precision.

questions.prompt: Three distinct simulated systems have weights 1, 2 and 5; only the second and third form merging compact binaries. Their total weighted yield is:
questions.hint: Sum weights only over the successful systems.
questions.feedback: The successful systems contribute 2+5=7 weight units, whereas their raw number is two.

questions.prompt: In two unbiased Monte Carlo samples from the same distribution, increasing sample size from N to 4N changes the approximate standard error of a simple sample mean by a factor of:
questions.hint: Under ordinary finite-variance IID assumptions, SE scales as 1/sqrt(N).
questions.feedback: SE(4N)/SE(N)=sqrt(N/(4N))=1/2; weighted/non-IID simulations need more careful variance treatment.

questions.prompt: A toy simulation samples 200 distinct binaries, of which 20 meet a stated outcome criterion. The unweighted sample fraction is:
questions.hint: Divide successes by total sampled systems, not by event rows.
questions.feedback: 20/200=0.10. This sample fraction is not automatically a cosmic merger rate or a mass-normalized formation efficiency.

objectives.title: Trace sensitivity and survivorship
objectives.evidence: Explain how model parameters propagate to output populations.

questions.prompt: If a code changes kick magnitude assumptions while keeping birth binaries and all other physics fixed, what outcome is most directly useful to compare?
choices: The observed detector population without modeling selection.
The surviving compact-binary yield and distribution of post-event orbital properties.
Only the terminal file's byte size.
questions.hint: Ask which physical transition kicks directly modify.
questions.feedback: Kicks alter post-supernova relative motion, survival and later evolution; comparing controlled populations isolates sensitivity to the chosen prescription.

questions.prompt: Why might preferentially oversampling rare massive binaries require weights?
choices: Weighting is needed only for optical telescope exposure time.
Otherwise sample counts would not represent the intended underlying birth distribution.
Oversampling guarantees unbiased cosmic rates without any correction.
questions.hint: Compare proposal distribution with target birth distribution.
questions.feedback: Importance or stratified sampling may need appropriate weights to recover target-population expectations.

questions.prompt: Why can a rare outcome disappear entirely in a small Monte Carlo run despite nonzero true model probability?
choices: A simulation must always produce every possible channel once.
Finite sampling can miss low-probability outcomes by chance.
Its probability must be exactly zero if unseen.
questions.hint: Recall that a random finite sample does not enumerate all possibilities.
questions.feedback: Low-count channels have large relative Monte Carlo uncertainty; zero sampled events does not by itself establish zero expected rate.

objectives.title: Critique population predictions
objectives.evidence: Distinguish numerical convergence, physical uncertainty and selection-biased comparisons.

questions.prompt: A result changes when the random seed changes in a small simulation. What should be investigated?
choices: Whether stochastic methods have invalidated probability theory.
Monte Carlo uncertainty and convergence across independent samples.
Which random seed gives the nicest-looking figure.
questions.hint: Random variation can be substantial for rare events.
questions.feedback: Compare replicate seeds/sample sizes and report sampling error before attributing differences to physical mechanisms.

questions.prompt: Two codes have different binary-merger yields. What comparison most helps identify an origin?
choices: Declare the code with more simulated systems physically correct.
Match initial distributions, prescriptions, definitions, weights and output selection before testing differences.
Compare only the number of lines in their source code.
questions.hint: Controlled code comparison needs matched inputs and outcome definitions.
questions.feedback: Different outputs may arise from sampling, normalization, physics prescriptions or implementation; matched setups and tests help disentangle them.

questions.prompt: A paper reports 50 successful binaries but no simulated formed mass or sampling method. What can't be deduced?
choices: That at least one system met the paper's reported criterion.
A properly normalized physical formation efficiency or cosmic event rate.
The raw count of 50.
questions.hint: An absolute yield needs a denominator and, often, weights.
questions.feedback: Raw successful-system counts lack birth-population normalization and are not rates per cosmic volume/time.

cases.title: Sample versus weight
cases.scenario: Five hypothetical systems have weights [1,4,2,3,5]; systems 2 and 5 produce the target event.
cases.task: Calculate the raw successful-system count and weighted yield, then identify the required denominator for a physical efficiency.
steps: Raw success count=2.
Weighted success yield=4+5=9.
A defined sampled/represented formed mass is needed for a mass-normalized formation efficiency.
cases.solution: The raw count 2 and weighted yield 9 answer different questions; neither alone is an astrophysical merger rate.

cases.title: Rare-event stability
cases.scenario: Independent simulation runs of 100, 1000 and 10000 systems find 0, 2 and 24 rare outcomes under one model.
cases.task: Explain whether the first zero disproves the modeled channel and name a convergence check.
steps: The first sample can miss a rare event by chance.
Fractions are 0, 0.002 and 0.0024.
Repeat seeds, increase N, and use uncertainty appropriate to sparse counts and weighting.
cases.solution: A zero in a small run is not proof of impossibility; investigate Monte Carlo precision and normalization.
